grh_2de8683b0a945979325e.title: Sorry to Let You Go
paragraphs: A middle-aged records-system manager is dismissed after a computer makes his job unnecessary, but he hides the loss from his wife and friends while desperately searching for comparable work. As savings and prospects disappear, he pays his life-insurance premium and begins thinking that his family may be better off if he is dead. After finally confessing that he has been unemployed for two months and feels like a failure, he is seriously injured in a car crash. He survives to discover that the people around him still value him, and during his recovery he finds a new use for the same skills that seemed obsolete: programming filing and record systems for computers. The story ends as he prepares to return to work, having learned that machines can replace tasks without replacing the value of people.

This [[show|theater-five|Theater Five]] broadcast aired on September 7, 1964. It is listed as episode 26 in the archive. [[org|org.0d7b5c86680811cc|ABC Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Ralph Camargo, Anne Seymour, Robert Dryden, Evie Juster, and Gilbert Mack. Other credited names include Ted Bell as director, Ian Martin as writer, and Fred Foy as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 25 minutes.

grh_2dc3c41f11a32f0ad3d0.title: Retribution
paragraphs: A husband and wife manufacture a phony western gold strike by planting ore, promoting a worthless mine and selling shares to eager townspeople. They intend to disappear after taking the money and even plan to destroy the workings so no one can prove the fraud. Instead, the blast exposes an enormous real vein of gold. The swindlers then discover that by selling every share they also gave away their rights to the land, leaving the investors owners of the genuine bonanza. Rather than share the fortune, the pair are left facing punishment and menial work at the very mine they tried to use as a fraud.

grh_2dcc4b9def053338ad28.title: Angies Last Cure
paragraphs: Angie Hopper becomes an obsessive hypochondriac after buying a popular book of symptoms, diagnosing herself with one illness after another and keeping exhausted husband Fred constantly waiting on her. Dr. Christian sees that arguing with her fears will accomplish nothing. When Fred develops an ordinary ache, Angie immediately transfers all her attention to him, and Dr. Christian quietly encourages the reversal by giving Fred's harmless baldness the impressive name of a chronic glabrous condition. Caring for Fred cures Angie of her own imaginary diseases so completely that she throws the symptom book into the fire.

grh_2d128e06a5530d91e5df.title: Story Of Prisoners Child
paragraphs: Seven-year-old Patty Elliott is gravely ill, with her mother dead and her devoted father Walt in prison for an old theft he voluntarily confessed to years after rebuilding his life. Convinced that medicine alone will not save the child, Dr. Christian races to the state capital and refuses to accept the normal timetable for parole, arguing that Walt's return is urgently part of Patty's treatment. After an exhausting overnight fight for his release, Dr. Christian brings Walt home. Patty, whom another doctor believed might not survive the morning, revives almost immediately once her father is beside her.

The chief rejects Gene's warning and modern veterinary methods, trusting traditional protection instead, so Gene seeks help from the chief's college-educated son Charlie. Charlie tries to bridge the two viewpoints but becomes gravely ill after eating meat from an infected steer; with a fever around 105 degrees his heart briefly stops and the medicine man believes he has died. A doctor gives Charlie an emergency injection and revives him, giving the chief direct evidence of the value of modern medicine while the broadcast returns to music.

This recording comes from Melody Ranch.

Gene Autry western musical-variety series combining songs, comedy and a dramatic Western segment.
